titre: Miranda: the confession is thrown out, the conviction comes back
accroche: Phoenix, 1966: the Supreme Court overturns Ernesto Miranda's conviction over a poorly obtained confession. In 1967, he is convicted again, without it.
contenu_vulgarise:
On March 13, 1963, Phoenix, Arizona police arrest Ernesto Miranda at his home. A young woman has been kidnapped and raped; she identifies him at the station. Two officers question him in Interrogation Room No. 2. About two hours later, they come out with a written confession, signed in his own hand. At trial, they acknowledge not having told him he had the right to have a lawyer with him.

Miranda is found guilty of kidnapping and rape. He is sentenced to twenty to thirty years in prison on each of the two counts, the sentences to run concurrently.

## The confession the Court pulls from the record

On June 13, 1966, the U.S. Supreme Court overturns that conviction, in an opinion written by its Chief Justice, Warren. It does not say Miranda is innocent. It holds that statements made by a man questioned in custody can be used against him only if the prosecution proves he was surrounded by safeguards protecting his right not to incriminate himself. The ruling lists what he must be told before any questioning: that he has the right to remain silent, that anything he says can be used against him in court, that he has the right to have a lawyer present, and that one will be appointed for him if he cannot afford one. The form Miranda signed was not enough to prove that he had knowingly waived these rights.

## The second trial

The case goes back to the Arizona courts, which try Miranda again. The trial begins on February 15, 1967, before Judge Lawrence K. Wren. The county prosecutor, Robert Corbin, can no longer rely on the confession. He has another witness: Twila Hoffman, Miranda's partner. According to Encyclopedia.com, she came forward during a custody dispute over their daughter, and she recounts a conversation held with him after his arrest, in which he admitted the rape. The defense argues that a partner cannot testify against him; Judge Wren rules that she can. On March 1, 1967, Miranda is again found guilty and sentenced, as in 1963, to twenty to thirty years in prison.

He is paroled in 1972. On January 31, 1976, at age 34, he is stabbed in a fight at the Amapola bar in Phoenix. The man charged with the murder a few days later fled to Mexico, where he has never been found.

## The shift

We often hear that a procedural flaw sets a guilty man free. In the case that gave the rule its name, procedure threw out a piece of evidence, not the prosecution. The Court ruled on how evidence is obtained, not on what Miranda had done, and a second jury was able to rule on a different piece of evidence. The two questions come apart: irregular evidence is not false evidence, and its exclusion is not an acquittal. What remains is the 1967 piece of evidence: a witness recounting what a man told her in private, and that no one else heard.

repere.texte: On June 13, 1966, the U.S. Supreme Court holds that statements obtained from an accused in custody can be used against him only if the prosecution proves effective safeguards of his right not to incriminate himself, and for that reason overturns the conviction of Ernesto Miranda, arrested on March 13, 1963.
repere.source: Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966), U.S. Supreme Court, opinion of Chief Justice Warren

carte.punch: His confession is thrown out in 1966. In 1967, Miranda is convicted again, without it.
carte.idee: In 1966, the Supreme Court throws out Ernesto Miranda's confession, obtained without his rights being read to him. Retried in 1967 on the testimony of his partner, he is convicted again and sentenced to twenty to thirty years in prison.
carte.source_courte: Miranda v. Arizona, U.S. Supreme Court, 1966

quiz.question: What does the Supreme Court decide in 1966 about Miranda's confession, and what then becomes of the accused?
choix: It clears him because the signed confession was false, and Miranda is freed without a new trial
It upholds the confession but orders a new trial to review the sentence handed down
It throws out the confession for lack of safeguards, and Miranda is convicted again in 1967 on other testimony
It voids the trial because the jury was improperly composed, without ruling on the confession
quiz.explication: The 1966 ruling concerns how the confession was obtained, not guilt: the Court neither finds the confession false nor Miranda innocent, and it does not uphold the confession. Nor does it rely on the composition of the jury. Retried in 1967 without the confession, Miranda is convicted again, notably on the testimony of his partner.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What safeguards does the 1966 ruling require before any custodial interrogation?
choix: The right to remain silent and the right to a lawyer, appointed if need be
The right to be tried within 48 hours of arrest
The right to have a family member present during the interrogation
The right to immediately appeal any recorded statement
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1966 ruling requires that the accused be informed of his right to remain silent and his right to a lawyer, appointed if he cannot afford one, before any custodial interrogation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is Miranda's new conviction in 1967 based on?
choix: A second signed confession, obtained this time with the required warnings
The testimony of Twila Hoffman, his partner, recounting a conversation after the arrest
New forensic analyses that were absent from the first trial
The victim's identification, repeated before the second jury
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Without the confession thrown out in 1966, the second trial relies on Twila Hoffman, Miranda's partner, who recounts a conversation held with him after his arrest.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Judge Wren decide about Twila Hoffman's testimony?
choix: He postpones the trial to verify the witness's identity
He excludes it, finding that a partner cannot testify against the accused
He asks Twila Hoffman to testify in writing only
He rules it admissible, over the defense's objection
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Judge Wren rules Twila Hoffman's testimony admissible against Miranda, over the objection of the defense, which argued that a partner could not testify against him.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What becomes of Ernesto Miranda after his parole in 1972?
choix: He is stabbed in 1976 in a fight at the Amapola bar
He is arrested again in 1976 for armed robbery
He dies of illness in 1976, after serving his sentence
He is cleared at a new trial in 1976, on DNA evidence
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On January 31, 1976, at age 34, Miranda is stabbed in a fight at the Amapola bar in Phoenix; the man charged with the murder later fled to Mexico, where he has never been found.
